title: Before Sunday's Futures Open, Traders Are Pricing a December Hike Around the October CPI Report
dek: The October consumer price report on Tuesday is the test of whether the Fed's rate-hike debate has room to cool. Here is what the data will and won't show, and what markets are already pricing.
author: Meridian Newsroom

image.alt: Black-and-white photograph of an automatic ticker apparatus on the New York Stock Exchange trading floor
image.credit: Library of Congress via Wikimedia Commons

keyPoints: The October CPI is due Tuesday, Nov. 10, at 8:30 a.m. ET, and the September reading was 3.7% from a year earlier (Stock Titan; Kiplinger).
BLS will not publish a 12-month rate for overall or core prices this month, because October 2025 prices were never collected (Stock Titan, citing BLS).
Cleveland Fed nowcast: about +0.24% on the month for October, against +0.6% in September (Stock Titan, citing the Cleveland Fed).
CME FedWatch odds of a quarter-point hike in December were about 81% in a Kiplinger snapshot from the week's preview (Kiplinger).
body:
## What the Sunday open is pricing

Futures reopen Sunday evening after a week in which the Nasdaq Composite fell into correction, then rose 1.09% on Friday to 24,579.42, according to CNBC's live coverage. The question for the coming session is less about Friday's bounce than about rates. The labour data on Friday was firm, and traders have been pricing a higher chance of another Federal Reserve hike.

Kiplinger's weekly preview said CME Group's FedWatch tool showed futures traders pricing about 81% odds of a quarter-point hike at the December meeting. A CNBC write-up of the October jobs report put the figure at 76.8% after that release. The two numbers were taken at different times, so neither should be read as a live quote.

## Why this CPI report reads differently

The normal yearly inflation rate will be missing. Stock Titan, citing the Bureau of Labor Statistics, reports that October 2025 prices were never collected during the government shutdown. That means the overall and core year-over-year rates people usually quote will not be published on Tuesday. The one-month changes will still come out.

The last published yearly figure is 3.7% for September, according to Stock Titan and Kiplinger. Kiplinger's staff economist expects the annual rate to end the year at about 4%. Barclays expects headline CPI to have risen 0.2% on the month in October, about 40 basis points below September's increase, with gasoline leading the reprieve.

## What traders will watch

The monthly core reading matters most. Barclays expects a moderation in core inflation after two months of upside surprises. A soft core print would ease pressure on the December hike case; a firm one would push that case higher.

The Fed's December 9 decision, as Stock Titan notes, is the policy event this report feeds into. Rates-sensitive shares and the dollar are likely to react first, and the Treasury curve will show the view before equities do.

## Why it matters for the open

Because the yearly rate is missing, some traders may lean harder on the monthly core figure and on Cleveland Fed-style nowcasts. That makes the reaction more sensitive to small surprises than a normal report would be.

This is an explainer of how the report is structured and how markets are positioned. It is not a forecast of the outcome, and the consensus figures above come from the sources named.

marketImpact.summary: The December hike case is the main macro driver into Tuesday. A monthly core print that undershoots would support yields lower and rate-sensitive stocks; an upside surprise would strengthen the hike case and weigh on growth and chip names that already sold off this week.
marketImpact.timeframe: Sunday evening futures open through Tuesday's 8:30 a.m. ET CPI release

tickers.rationale: Long-dated Treasuries react first to the monthly core print and the hike-odds shift
Nasdaq-heavy growth exposure is most sensitive to a firmer inflation read
A hawkish surprise would likely support the dollar
